episode_thesis: Cory Hoffstein and Adam Butler (Return Stacked) argue that portable alpha, packaged as capital-efficient ETFs ('return stacking'), lets investors keep core stock and bond beta while adding diversifying return streams such as trend, carry and merger arbitrage. Their trend product replicates the SG Trend Index beta cheaply by blending a bottom-up fitted trend model (70%) with a top-down regression on recent index returns (30%), because the two have comparable fit but weakly correlated tracking errors; generic trend beta is becoming a commodity that performance-fee managers must beat with differentiated, fat-tail, or faster strategies.

speakers.name: Cory Hoffstein
speakers.role: Co-founder, Return Stacked Portfolio Solutions (joint venture) and Newfound Research; product designer of the ETF suite
speakers.speaker_note: Captions give no names, so attribution rests on dialogue cues. Several passages were corrected in the ledger to Cory (C07-3 data window, C09-2 fat-tail attenuation, C13-2 and C13-3 high-vol overlay and client tolerance); those corrections are applied here. Where a passage runs on without a visible change of speaker, attribution is uncertain.

worldview_premises.premise: Portable alpha (return stacking) lets investors keep core stock and bond beta and free capital through futures and swaps for other alpha sources; it has been an institutional tool for about 40 years and a ticker packages it for people who will not run a derivatives book.
worldview_premises.support: History from PIMCO in the 1980s; his own career building alternatives.

worldview_premises.premise: Selling alternatives by asking investors to sell some core stocks and bonds repeatedly disappointed in the 2010s (non-stop US 60/40 outperformance); a capital-efficient stack removes that behavioural obstacle.
Dispersion among trend managers comes from implementation choices (markets, speeds, risk weights, constraints); fitting parameters to the index removes arbitrary dispersion and delivers 'trend beta'.

The SG Trend Index is made of the largest managers, whose less liquid markets matter little to P&L, so a limited-market replication tracks them well; around 80% of their risk sits in the same ~20 markets and fat-tail weights average toward zero across managers.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning from managers' scale; coffee in 2023-24 as an idiosyncratic bet that averaged out.

worldview_premises.premise: Fitting trend weights needs 15-20 years of data because markets can contribute no P&L for a decade, making it impossible to tell untraded markets from untrending ones; annual reruns will not change weights meaningfully.
worldview_premises.support: Training on 2000-10 versus 2010-20 gives different market weights.

worldview_premises.premise: A top-down regression is flexible and captures manager innovation and unobserved markets but is backward-looking, blind to positions in markets with no recent P&L, and untethered mechanically from trend following.
worldview_premises.support: Example of the 2023 regional bank crisis when managers flipped bond positions within 2-3 days; Swiss franc approximated by gold and euro.

worldview_premises.premise: A bottom-up model and a top-down regression track the trend index about equally well but have weakly correlated tracking errors, so blending 30% top-down and 70% bottom-up lowers aggregate tracking error; the blend is still a trend following strategy.
worldview_premises.support: Tracking error and correlation results quoted (tracking-error correlation about 0.2-0.3 in the captions).

worldview_premises.premise: Top-down regression struggles with fast multi-day mean-reversion models in the broader CTA index, so replicating the CTA index bottom-up is harder than replicating the trend index; Andrew Beer's fund uses only top-down.

Generic trend beta can be bought in QIS for 10-15 bp, so performance-fee managers must differentiate (spreads, breakouts, speed, fat-tail markets); generic trend managers will be squeezed out by cheaper implementations.
worldview_premises.support: Conversations with institutions buying trend beta from banks.

worldview_premises.premise: A longer tail of markets raises Sharpe but diverts risk from markets tied to big macro factors, reducing the crisis offset (citing Quantica).
A high-volatility trend strategy is a capital-efficient version of a low-vol one, but most clients cannot tolerate more than about 10% vol (citing Cliff Asness), so products moved to 10-12% vol.
Stack only low-correlation components (equity plus trend); regulation (SEC Rule 18f-4: 20-day 99% VaR capped at 20% or 2x the benchmark) limits how far stacking can be pushed.

Merger arbitrage earns a spread consisting of time value of money plus a deal-break risk premium (about 200-250 bp over SOFR in 20 years) with low correlation to equity, bond and credit premia (about 0.5 to credit).
worldview_premises.support: Generic strategy history; no source cited.

worldview_premises.premise: An ETF cannot be closed, so the strategy must run identically at small and large size; at extreme scale performance would degrade and self-correct.
worldview_premises.support: Structural fact of ETFs; wants track record continuity.

worldview_premises.premise: Diversifying strategies (trend, carry, merger) and diversifying assets (gold, Bitcoin) are different overlay buckets for stock-bond portfolios; gold and Bitcoin are a store-of-value diversifier.
Futures-based ETF trend products use a subset of the most liquid US and European markets versus the full set in mutual fund and hedge fund versions.

mechanism_chains.topic: Merger arbitrage as a stacked return stream

steps.from: Deal announced at a buyout price
steps.to: target trades below the price
steps.why: Time value of money plus deal-break credit-like risk.

steps.from: Capture the spread
steps.to: about 200-250 bp over SOFR historically with low correlation to other risk premia

decision_process.practice: Offer building blocks that stack an overlay on a core exposure (equity plus trend, bond plus trend, bond plus merger, equity plus multi-asset carry, equity plus gold and Bitcoin) so wealth managers build portfolios.
decision_process.why: Keep beta, add diversifiers without giving up core.

decision_process.practice: Replicate the SG Trend Index with a 70% bottom-up fitted trend model and 30% top-down robust regression, rebalanced daily.
decision_process.why: Blend lowers tracking error and adds process diversification.

decision_process.practice: Run 26-27 liquid futures markets spanning equity, bond, commodity and currency; keep the same universe at all sizes; use back-month contracts to expand capacity beyond CFTC front-month limits.
decision_process.why: Replicates the full universe closely; ETF cannot close.

decision_process.practice: Fit trend weights using 15-20 years of data and cross-validation; rerun annually without expecting material weight changes; check for systematic drift in trend length.
decision_process.why: Shorter windows give unstable market weights.

decision_process.practice: Trade the ETF as a one-way buy and hold; use institutional desks for NAV-based or risk quotes for size; accept 20-30 bp spreads for small trades.
decision_process.why: Market makers widen quotes when they cannot see the basket.

decision_process.practice: Stack only low-correlation components; respect SEC Rule 18f-4 VaR limits; rebalance nightly; keep collateral for the trend overlay at 25-30% of NAV with a cash buffer.
decision_process.why: Ruin risk negligible and margin does not force sales in a drawdown.

decision_process.practice: Target trend volatility of about 10-13.5% (stack on S&P with a 13.5% vol trend system) because clients cannot tolerate more.
decision_process.why: Line-item risk too large above about 10% vol.

decision_process.practice: Use the mutual fund version for a wider and more diverse set of futures markets than the ETF; ETF wrapper for tax advantage and intraday access.
decision_process.why: ETF market-maker hedging limits illiquid markets.

decision_process.practice: Merger arbitrage via a licensed machine-learning index of US-listed deals that clear a hurdle rate, hedged short or via swaps for stock components.
decision_process.why: Systematic deal selection; avoids borrow risk.

speakers.evidence_style: Backtest-style replication statistics (correlation about 0.8, tracking error, cross-validation), design rationale and regulatory/operational detail; cites others' research (Quantica, Asness) from memory; reasoning about industry structure and fees.

current_views.view: Replication ETFs form a fair, cheap benchmark; generic trend with performance fees will be squeezed; differentiation lies in the fat tail, spreads and breakouts.
current_views.reasoning: Trend beta available for 10-15 bp in QIS.

current_views.view: Gold and Bitcoin overlay on US equity is a store-of-value diversifier for a stock-bond portfolio; gold in particular a long-term diversifier.
current_views.reasoning: Thematic store-of-value narrative; diversifying assets bucket.

current_views.view: Merger arbitrage is a diversifying return stream worth stacking on bonds.
current_views.reasoning: Low correlation to equity, bond and credit premia.

current_views.view: April 2025: a drawdown in the CTA space after equities fell; may be early innings with recovery in 30-50 days (host view); the stacks showed no dislocation.

speakers.name: Adam Butler
speakers.role: Co-founder, Return Stacked Portfolio Solutions; Resolve Asset Management Global (futures-based alternatives, risk parity and active strategies)
speakers.speaker_note: Captions give no speaker labels; attribution follows dialogue cues and ledger corrections (C07-3, C09-2, C13-2, C13-3 moved to Cory). Adam leads the bid-ask, bottom-up regression, validation and margin-management answers.

worldview_premises.premise: Mutual fund wrappers can trade a wider futures set than ETFs because ETF market makers need liquid hedges for creations and redemptions; the choice is a trade-off between tax efficiency, intraday liquidity and platform access versus market breadth.

Spreads of small ETF trades in a less liquid futures basket average 20-30 bp and widen in stress, and are persistent because market makers cannot see the basket; large trades through institutional desks can be done near NAV, and a long holding period smooths the cost.

Any fund faces a capacity trade-off: more diverse bets raise expected performance but liquidity limits what can trade at size; CFTC front-month limits can be bypassed using back-month contracts for 10x or more capacity.

A 26-27 market universe covering equities, bonds, commodities and currencies (70-80% of global futures liquidity) replicates the full CTA universe closely because all players trade in proportion to liquidity; he admits being surprised.

A grid of time-series momentum lookbacks (5-300 days per market) can span continuous moving-average-crossover rules, so regressing on it can mimic them; breakout systems with trailing stops and entry-only vol scaling have far more degrees of freedom and are not spanned.
The bottom-up replication gets about 0.8 daily correlation to the SG Trend Index (an average of 10 funds with different styles).

Fitted market weights change by decade (S&P trendless in 2000-10, trendy 2010-20) but sector weights and trend speeds are stable under cross-validation, and there is no evidence that trend length rose systematically over 2000-2020 (considered 'largely mythical').

Top-down is kept as an expression of epistemological humility: managers constantly innovate and it captures idiosyncratic methods the continuous bottom-up misses, even though the bottom-up has the better average fit.
worldview_premises.support: Comparison of fit on the trend index.

worldview_premises.premise: Carry, skewness, seasonality and relative-value features improve the fit to the broader CTA index far more than to the trend index, where the gain is marginal.

Nightly rebalancing keeps the beta/trend ratio fixed after losses; trend collateral needs only 25-30% of NAV with a 40-50% cash buffer, so risk of ruin is negligible, as seen in the April 2025 drawdown.
worldview_premises.support: Audit of performance, margin use and balance in April 2025.

steps.why: Weights on long and short averages replicate crossovers.

steps.from: Result

steps.from: Check across training windows
steps.to: sector weights and speeds stable

worldview_premises.premise: Replication ETFs form a cheap benchmark that performance-fee hedge funds must beat over the long run; market forces squeezing generic trend managers are 'fair and square'.

Trend funds now run 8-12% volatility, so returns lack the punch of 1980s-90s CTAs, trading off stress payoff; investors can no longer tolerate 20-25% volatility whereas 25 years ago equities at 20% volatility were fine.
A levered risk-parity bond and equity allocation and some QIS products already work as portable alpha, so investors may hold the concept unknowingly.

disagreements.topic: Relative quality of top-down versus bottom-up replication

positions.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
positions.position: Both replicate the trend index about equally well (statistically indistinguishable) and the top-down works though it is mechanically untethered from trend; blend them for lower tracking error.

positions.speaker: Adam Butler
positions.position: The bottom-up has the better average fit track record, but the top-down sometimes overwhelms it by catching idiosyncratic manager methods, which is why it is kept.

disagreements.topic: Whether a replication is 'divorced from trend following'

positions.speaker: Critics (as characterised by Cory)
positions.position: Replication is totally divorced from trend following.

positions.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
positions.position: The 70% bottom-up leg applies true trend signals fitted to the index and the 30% top-down leg adds process diversification.

disagreements.topic: Value of a long tail of markets

positions.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
positions.position: The ETF delivers trend beta with a handful of common markets; a longer tail raises Sharpe but weakens crisis offset; fat-tail trading is for managers adding alpha.

positions.speaker: Moritz (co-hosts)
positions.position: They like trading fat-tail and alternative markets, spreads and punchier returns; the question is how much stress payoff you want.

disagreements.topic: Recalibration of a fixed bottom-up fit

positions.speaker: Moritz (co-hosts)
positions.position: A fixed fit has no response function if managers change speed or markets.

positions.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
positions.position: It is non-trivial; 15-20 years are needed and annual reruns will not change weights meaningfully.

positions.speaker: Adam Butler
positions.position: Sector weights and speeds were stable in cross-validation and no systematic lengthening of trend speeds was found.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Speaker attribution is uncertain for several passages (ledger corrections move C07-3, C09-2, C13-2, C13-3 to Cory).

The 0.8 daily correlation is in-sample against an average of 10 funds; the quoted tracking-error correlation (about 2.3 in the captions, likely 0.2-0.3) is garbled and no out-of-sample figure is given.

Fitting needs 15-20 years but the weights are said to be stable under cross-validation; training on 2000-10 versus 2010-20 gave different market weights, so stability applies only at sector and speed level.
Claim that 26-27 markets replicate the full universe 'closely' is not quantified.
Spread estimates of 20-30 bp are given as typical without data and assume small trades.
Merger arbitrage return (200-250 bp over SOFR) and correlation of 0.5 to credit are stated without sources.
Whether adding carry, skew, seasonality features to the bottom-up model is justified is left open: marginal against the trend index but material against the CTA index.
The statement that ETF performance would 'self-correct' at $20bn or more is unsupported by capacity analysis.
Top-down regression blind spots (no P&L in markets over the lookback) are acknowledged, with only a vague 'things you can do to manage around that'.
Claim that stacking ruin risk is negligible rests on one April 2025 episode.
Gold and Bitcoin are treated as diversifying assets with a store-of-value narrative but no evidence is given.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) The speakers are product builders rather than forecasters. Observable inputs they use: the daily SG Trend Index and the CTA index returns (regressed on a recent 20-40 day window), fitted risk weights by sector (about 25% each), trend speeds (intermediate), merger-arbitrage spread and deal-close probability features, and bid-ask spreads and NAV premia for ETF execution. They offer no price forecasts; the April 2025 hope for a trend recovery in 30-50 days is a host remark.
reader_inferences: (reader) The central argument is that trend 'beta' is largely determined by a small set of common markets and speeds, so it is replicable and will be priced like beta; alpha is claimed only in the fat tail and differentiated design.
(reader) The 30/70 blend is a process-diversification decision: neither method is shown to dominate, and the blend reduces tracking error by combining weakly correlated errors.
(reader) The guests have a commercial interest in the replication and stacking products, so claims about the adequacy of limited universes and negligible ruin risk are framed by that interest.
(reader) Several mechanics (SEC 18f-4 VaR cap, CFTC front-month limits, ETF creation/redemption) bound the design, so practical constraints rather than signal quality drive many choices.
